1131.event_title: W. B. Yeats proposes to Maud Gonne and is refused
1131.event: The Irish poet W. B. Yeats met Maud Gonne in 1889 and fell in love with her; she admired and liked him but did not return his love, and he courted her for nearly three decades. He dedicated his play The Countess Kathleen (1892) to her and wrote Cathleen ni Houlihan (1902) with her in the title role. In 1899 he asked her to marry him and she declined, and in 1903 she married Major John MacBride.
1131.explanation: Turned down in private, Yeats kept declaring his love in public through plays and poems that all Ireland could see.
1131.tie_back: Like the refused lover in this kural who has no shelter left except to ride the palm-stem horse in the street, Yeats, denied in private, made his hopeless love a public matter.
1131._accuracy_note: The refused, long-suffering lover who turns to public display matches the madal idea, but Yeats's dedications were not a deliberate attempt to shame Gonne's family into consent; this event is also already used once elsewhere in the book (chapter 120).

1132.event_title: Longfellow persists after Fanny Appleton refuses him
1132.place: Boston and Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States
1132.event: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, a young widower, fell in love with Frances (Fanny) Appleton after travelling with her family in Switzerland. He was crushed when she rejected his marriage proposal in 1837, but he did not give up. She accepted him in the spring of 1843, and they married in July 1843; her father gave the couple Craigie House as a wedding gift.
1132.explanation: A respected professor and poet kept up a suit that had already been refused, accepting the embarrassment of pressing on for six years.
1132.tie_back: The kural's lover says that body and life can no longer bear the pain and so shame must be set aside; Longfellow likewise set aside the pride of a rejected suitor and kept pursuing the woman he loved.
1132._accuracy_note: Shows persistence after refusal, but nothing like a public act of shame is documented, so the fit to 'setting shame aside' is partial.

1133.event_title: John Donne's secret marriage costs him his career
1133.event: In December 1601 the poet John Donne, then secretary to the powerful Sir Thomas Egerton, secretly married the seventeen-year-old Ann More. When Donne told her father months later, Sir George More demanded his dismissal; Donne lost his post in 1602 and was briefly imprisoned. The marriage was upheld, but Donne found no regular employment for more than twelve years and lived on the help of friends, relatives and patrons.
1133.explanation: A rising young man of standing exchanged his position and reputation for the woman he loved.
1133.tie_back: As the kural's lover says that he once had good name and honourable manhood and now has only his love, Donne's love left him with his wife but without the career and standing he had once enjoyed.
1133._accuracy_note: A clear case of love stripping a man of his former standing, though Donne's loss came from a secret marriage rather than from a public display like the madal.

1134.event_title: Emperor Xuanzong's devotion to Yang Guifei and the An Lushan Rebellion
1134.event: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, whose early reign brought reforms and the start of a golden age, came under the influence of his consorts in later life, above all Yang Guifei, and withdrew more and more from government while her relatives gained high posts. In 755 the general An Lushan rebelled, and Xuanzong fled the capital Chang'an with Yang Guifei and her family. During the flight his own troops demanded her death, the emperor consented, and he soon gave up the throne to his son.
1134.explanation: A ruler once known for wise government let attachment carry away his judgement and his sense of duty, with grave results for his empire.
1134.tie_back: The kural says the fierce flood of love sweeps away the raft of restraint and honour; Xuanzong's passion swept away the careful rule that had once made his reign famous.
1134._accuracy_note: Historians agree that Xuanzong withdrew from government under his consorts' influence, but traditional accounts that blame Yang Guifei for the rebellion are partly moralising, and the tragic ending goes beyond the kural; already used once elsewhere in the book (chapter 91).

1135.event_title: Ivan Turgenev follows the singer Pauline Viardot abroad
1135.place: St Petersburg, Russia; Paris, France; Baden-Baden, Germany
1135.event: The Russian writer Ivan Turgenev fell in love with the singer Pauline Viardot when she first performed in Russia in 1843. In 1847 he left Russia for Paris with the Viardot circle and stayed there until 1850, and he later moved to Baden-Baden in Germany to be near her again. He wrote the libretto for her operetta Le dernier sorcier (1869) and spent his last years at Bougival near Paris.
1135.explanation: One meeting with a singer reshaped the whole course of a great writer's life and kept him far from home for decades.
1135.tie_back: In the kural the lover says that the girl with the small bangles has given him both the palm-stem horse and the sorrow of every evening; Turgenev's love for one woman likewise gave him a lifetime of devotion and longing.
1135._accuracy_note: Captures a lifelong love that one woman caused, but the 'evening sorrow' is an interpretation, since the sources do not describe Turgenev's feelings in detail; already used once elsewhere in the book (chapter 120).

1136.event_title: Kafka's hundreds of letters to Felice Bauer
1136.place: Prague (now Czech Republic) and Berlin, Germany
1136.event: Franz Kafka met Felice Bauer on 13 August 1912 at the home of his friend Max Brod in Prague and wrote her his first letter on 20 September 1912. Over the next five years he sent her more than five hundred letters and postcards, a romance carried on mostly on paper because they met in person only rarely. They were engaged twice, first in 1914, and both engagements were broken off; the final break came in 1917.
1136.explanation: Kafka's restless letter-writing shows how a love that cannot be settled keeps the mind turning over the same longing again and again.
1136.tie_back: The kural's lover cannot close his eyes even at midnight for thinking of the girl; Kafka's flood of letters shows the same sleepless, unending preoccupation with a beloved he could neither win nor give up.
1136._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the obsession fits, but the sources do not document sleeplessness, and the couple were engaged, not refused as in the kural; already used once elsewhere in the book (chapter 118); the two sources differ slightly on the year of the second engagement.

1137.event_title: Princess Margaret announces she will not marry Peter Townsend
1137.event: Princess Margaret, sister of Queen Elizabeth II, wished to marry Group Captain Peter Townsend, a former equerry who was divorced, at a time when the Church of England did not accept remarriage after divorce. Townsend was posted abroad as an air attaché, and after they met again in October 1955 she issued a public statement that she had decided not to marry him. In it she cited the Church's teaching that Christian marriage is indissoluble and her duty to the Commonwealth.
1137.explanation: A young woman bore a deep and long-standing love but chose restraint over defiance, and made the choice herself in public.
1137.tie_back: The kural praises the woman who suffers a love as vast as the sea yet never rides the palm-stem horse; Margaret kept her love within the limits she felt bound by rather than breaking them openly.
1137._accuracy_note: A strong picture of a woman's restraint under great love, though her reasons were religious and constitutional, and later documents suggest a marriage might have been possible if she gave up her succession rights.

1138.event_title: Crown Prince Harald's secret romance with Sonja Haraldsen becomes public
1138.event: Crown Prince Harald of Norway and Sonja Haraldsen, who was not of royal descent, were a couple for several years before the relationship became public; rumours of a girlfriend he wished to marry spread in 1967 and 1968. The press and public then debated whether a commoner could become queen, and Harald made clear that if he could not marry Sonja he would consider staying unmarried for life. After about nine years together King Olav V consented, and they married in Oslo Cathedral on 29 August 1968.
1138.explanation: A love kept quiet for years could not stay hidden forever, and once it came out it was argued over by the whole nation.
1138.tie_back: The kural says love does not stop to weigh restraint but breaks out of its secrecy into the public square; Harald and Sonja's long-hidden love ended up debated across all of Norway.
1138._accuracy_note: Fits the movement from secrecy to public talk very well, though the couple's restraint was long and deliberate rather than overwhelmed.

1139.event_title: Chagall paints himself floating to kiss Bella in Birthday
1139.event: In July 1915, on the occasion of Marc Chagall's birthday, Bella Rosenfeld came to his room in Vitebsk with food and flowers wrapped in embroidered shawls. Chagall painted the scene as Birthday, showing himself floating in the air to kiss her; the oil-on-cardboard painting is now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. The two married on 25 July 1915, though her family still had doubts about the match.
1139.explanation: Chagall turned his private joy into an image so open and exuberant that it has been shown to the world ever since.
1139.tie_back: The kural pictures love as if it were wandering bewildered through the streets so that everyone will know of it; Chagall's floating lovers show the same giddy love that cannot stay hidden.
1139._accuracy_note: Next-best: the joy and public display fit, but the painting celebrates happy love rather than the bewildered, unhappy love of the kural; already used once elsewhere in the book (chapter 111), and sources differ on whether his birthday was 6 or 7 July.

1140.event_title: Richard and Mildred Loving are convicted for their marriage
1140.event: Richard Loving, who was white, and Mildred Jeter, who was of African American and Native American descent, married in Washington, D.C., on 2 June 1958 and returned home to Caroline County, Virginia, where interracial marriage was illegal. Weeks later the sheriff arrested them at home in the early morning, and in January 1959 they pleaded guilty and were sentenced to a year in prison, suspended on condition that they leave Virginia. In 1967 the United States Supreme Court unanimously struck the law down in Loving v. Virginia.
1140.explanation: Officials who had no understanding of the couple's love treated it as a crime, and only years later did the nation's highest court see it differently.
1140.tie_back: The kural's lover says thoughtless people mock him because they have never suffered as he has; the Lovings were judged and punished by people who did not understand what their love meant to them.
1140._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the Lovings faced legal condemnation rather than laughter, so the event is far graver than the kural's complaint about mockery.
